items.title: Imagine Every AI Agent on Earth Buying the Same Cheap Paper Towels
items.description: C lose your eyes, and imagine a frictionless day. You wake up to a notification that a grocery-store employee will deliver all of the ingredients for the three recipes you saved last night to your “Weeknight Dinner” folder. While you brew your coffee, a program browses online retailers to compare toilet-paper prices, and another solicits competitive bids for Sheetrock work you need done in the garage. During your commute, a bot moves your upcoming dentist appointment to avoid a scheduling conflict. On your lunch break, you get an alert that computers acting on your behalf noticed some unclaimed funds and class-action payouts in a state database and claimed them. Also, the machine has negotiated a cheaper internet plan. By the time you get home, the groceries are on your doorstep, and you’ve gotten back $150. This is the future that OpenAI, Meta, xAI, Google, and the rest are selling with a spate of always-on AI assistants that work for you. “Imagine every person on earth with a second mind beyond their own,” Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, wrote of the company’s new AI helper, Muse. A few weeks after Muse’s launch, OpenAI launched its competing product, Dots, which Sam Altman claimed would let you “get more of your time and attention back.” [ Read: The singularity is not what it seems ] These AI agents promise to bulldoze the inefficiencies of daily life. Think about all of the opportunities you’re currently leaving on the table: You don’t change cell-service providers for a flash sale because of the paperwork involved. You haven’t fiddled with your 401(k) investments in years. You have kids to pick up, a date to dress for, sleep to catch up on. But your AI agents are different—they’re relentless, tireless, and shameless. They work in the background, without supervision, eagerly helping with all of these tasks and a bunch you didn’t even ask for. They use every tactic and loophole at their disposal to get you the best price and the highest-quality service because they’re able to pay attention to everything at once. The AI companies see a massive opportunity for hyper-personalized agents to become a new intermediary layer for the internet and the physical world. This future is already unfolding: People are giving Muse access to their phone number, email, credit cards, and bank accounts to make dinner reservations, contact customer service, and book vacations. Mark Zuckerberg says that he is using Muse to coach his martial-arts form and help him bake with his daughter (he isn’t very familiar with baking, being “normally into smoking meats”). Silicon Valley’s vision of boundless efficiency is shortsighted, or at least incomplete. Near the end of his blog post about Muse, Wang writes that “we’ve never seen humanity with every single person’s agency fully switched on.” He paints a utopian vision of laptop-class optimization. But such frictionless commerce, if it ever does come to pass, could bring about something else entirely: chaos. T he era of the agentic web started less than 24 months ago. Anthropic’s Claude Code, introduced in early 2025, allowed agents to write software and use other programs on your laptop. OpenClaw, launched later that same year, could navigate the web on your behalf. In the spring of 2026, Instinct, an invite-only app that let users text requests to a bot over iMessage or WhatsApp, began capturing the imagination of Silicon Valley insiders. It could book museum tickets, purchase gifts, and find in-network doctors. But it wasn’t until the launch of Meta’s Muse in early September that personalized agents hit the mainstream. Muse has been downloaded more than 5 million times in the past month and is especially popular among early adopters—entrepreneurs, investors, software developers. These users are now reporting back on their experiences and offering previews of our potential agentic future, which sounds both strange and jagged. When we reached out to Rajan Lukose, a start-up founder in the Bay Area, to discuss his use of AI assistants, he had his Muse set up a calendar invite. In the late 1990s and 2000s, Lukose worked for corporate research-and-development teams in Silicon Valley and did early research on web agents. Now, he told us, “they’re actually, finally becoming sort of real.” Lukose has been using Meta’s program for “annoying things that I would never do”: tracking travel sites over time to book the cheapest flights, submitting receipts for DoorDash credits, sorting out problems with a magazine subscription. “That’s something that’s a real pain in the ass that just gets done,” he said. Lukose said that the primary upside of using an agent is clawing back time and money. A few years ago, for instance, Lukose installed an automated tool that went through his Gmail, looked at various transactions, and filed claims under price-purchase guarantees. “That was like $600 that I just would not have gotten myself,” he said. The agentic era promises to deliver those kinds of savings to everyone. Decades ago, the internet was supposed to create perfect markets, with users able to compare the cost and quality of products and services from anywhere in the world. But it failed: People continued to make lots of decisions based on habit. That, in turn, is good for business. “A lot of things online are premised on limited human attention,” Andrey Fradkin, an economist at Boston University, told us. Digital advertisements, recommendation algorithms, brand reputation, and celebrity endorsements steered consumers toward making suboptimal purchases. AI agents are now here to finally fulfill the promise of perfect commerce. “The agent knows your preferences; they can go to every single platform, find the best products, the best deal for you, and then help you make that purchase,” Fradkin said. The agent won’t be fooled by sponsored posts or give up on shopping when they get distracted or hungry. “The current attention-based economy—if you gain the eyeball, you have a better chance to sell certain goods—that may change,” Ken Huang, who studies agentic AI at the University of San Francisco and runs an AI consultancy, told us. The bots are impervious to human-targeted nudges. Their attention is infinite. In the short term, however, this automated quest for efficiency is creating some unsettling dynamics. Over the past month, X, Reddit, and other forums have been overrun with examples of agents haggling customer-service representatives and contractors. Take the case of the Muse user Luke Whiting, who sent his agent to check on a prescription at Walgreens. Whiting, who works for an open-source-database company in San Francisco, told us that the pharmacist at the other end of the call refused to speak to an AI system. His Muse suggested that the best way forward would be for Whiting to abandon using the agent altogether: “Honest take: other stores might say the same thing,” it said. Having the Muse call other pharmacies “could just burn time. The fastest path is probably you calling yourself.” On a Subreddit for call-center employees, a recent thread is titled, in all caps, “I AM NOT AI.” “I have been asked 3 times this week ‘are you human?’” one person replied. Other users who identify themselves as call-center workers discuss their frustrations. One says that when customers question whether they’re talking to AI, they like to respond, “I’m a real boy,” like Pinocchio. Another, fed up with rude callers, vented, “Customers deserve ai.” Companies, meanwhile, are starting to tap AI systems to squeeze more out of their customers. According to Fradkin, many hospitals don’t charge as much as they could, simply because medical-billing codes are countless and labyrinthine. But using AI to document and code patient visits reliably allows hospitals to charge for more, and more expensive, services. That likely contributed to patient costs increasing by $650 million across Blue Cross Blue Shield from 2023 to 2025. And that’s only the beginning; health payments are projected to rise another 9 percent next year, largely because of AI billing. McDonald’s is reportedly using AI to analyze millions of consumer transactions and adjust prices at each location, for each menu item, based on local demand. (McDonald’s has said that its pricing portal is “a tool, not a mandate” to help franchisees.) It’s not hard to imagine vendors using AI to develop personalized, on-demand inventory management and dynamic pricing to maximize profits for streaming subscriptions, sports tickets, drug prescriptions, consumer electronics, insurance policies, and loans. This optimization assumes that the agents work as intended. So far, there have been plenty of stumbles: In a paper published earlier this year, a group of AI researchers found that agents, given assistant-style tasks in a virtual environment, leaked Social Security numbers and were easily hijacked by other people. Agents powered by Chinese models refused to complete tasks that involved politically sensitive topics. Two weeks ago, a tech executive’s AI agent randomly posted his financial information in a workplace chatroom for employees to see. Things could get weirder still: Tech companies market their agents as perfectly rational, when, in actuality, they can be extremely erratic and unpredictable. Sophia Kazinnik, who studies AI agents at Stanford, found some models to be overly generous and others to be exceedingly greedy. Across the board, they were far less patient than humans. When two personal AI agents are haggling over prices in the wild, the outcomes might not be maximally profitable. And there’s no assurance that all future agents will be created equal: More powerful models may have an upper hand in negotiations. Even if the agents are able to effectively shop and negotiate for us, important rules governing the privacy rights, liability, and economic allegiance associated with these tools will have to be codified. Does your Muse have a fiduciary responsibility to you, or a legal responsibility to Meta? If Muse pays for a $2,000 espresso machine instead of a $200 one, can you be refunded? If Muse leaks your account and routing numbers, is Chase required to refund any fraudulent payments? A t some point, everyone’s agents could reach parity. “Just like today, every business has a website and social-media accounts and email addresses and all these things, every business is going to have agents too,” Zuckerberg said in an interview this week. In this future, communication and commerce function almost entirely via computer proxies. Your agent calls a fancy restaurant for a dinner reservation, and a digital maître d’ picks up. Your agent and your insurer’s agent and your hospital’s agent all negotiate the price for your recent appointment. Prices fall, buyers and sellers are better matched, and businesses are incentivized to deliver higher-quality, customized services and products. This is “what economists dream about,” Fradkin said. But friction can serve a purpose for businesses. Banks make great sums when customers leave money in low-interest checking or savings accounts, and studies show that sizable portions of retailer subscription revenue are driven purely by “inertia,” another way of saying that people forget to cancel. (Friction can help consumers too: Inattention and incomplete information at times lead landlords, pharmacies, and other businesses to undercharge.) Our entire economy and basically every company are structured around the notion that humans have mental and physical limitations. Without them, existing market structures could collapse. “There’s this strange protection provided by the inefficiencies in our economy,” Rory Van Loo, a lawyer and a professor at the Wharton School, told us recently. In 2019, well before the rise of large language models, Van Loo envisioned a phenomenon he dubbed “digital market perfection.” Imagine everyone has a digital agent that is always looking for a lower price or a newer, better service. In this world, Van Loo argues, agents could, all at once, direct millions of consumers toward a new product or service—a process he calls “hyperswitching.” That would in theory be good news for consumers, but it would be sheer hell for companies. The nightmare scenario that Van Loo and others have conjured is a style of agentic bank run, where similarly attentive agents all pull money from a bank at once to get their clients better interest rates elsewhere. Maybe this sounds good or exciting to you—a kind of consumer’s revenge—but in practice, stable commercial markets would begin to look and function like the stock market. “If, all of a sudden, people could purchase whatever they wanted at the lowest price with the perfect ability to see every possible option, there’d be a lot of volatility in the world. It would seem highly efficient from an economic standpoint, but it could have devastating effects,” Van Loo said. Picture 1 million personal agents all switching their consumers to a new brand of paper towels on Amazon because a markdown made them three cents cheaper. The same Sweetgreen salad is $18 one week and $38 the next. Your electric bill is $150 one month and $450 the month after, and you’re uncertain with each payment whether your local utility is about to go bankrupt. “Stocks are bought and sold fast; markets change and plummet—such that we have a stop button for it, because it can go off the rails,” Van Loo noted. “But we don’t have those kinds of protections in most other markets.” There’s potential for collateral damage everywhere. If millions of people switching to higher-yield accounts causes a bank run, that’s a disaster for any person or institutional investor with money locked up at that bank. If half of Verizon’s customers switch to AT&T in one week to take advantage of a flash sale, the business could collapse overnight, affecting the other half of its customers. Sometimes, this rapid switching could signal healthy competition. Other times, it could cause organizations to implode. A world where AI proxies do the planning and talking could also mean a future where humans are constantly surprised by things they once were able to anticipate: a birthday present for your spouse ordered in a preposterous size that you must try to explain; a plumber showing up out of the blue. Or perhaps none of this will happen. It’s possible that an assistant-dominated economy turns out to be far more mundane, defined by tacked-on fees to keep the agents in check. Instead of agents allowing you to negotiate and bring down health-care, insurance, and electrical bills, the companies responsible for all of these services charge your agents every time they request to pull your data. Banks, to bolster their revenues in the event of a bank run, institute new and higher fees on checking accounts. Amazon, unable to profit from dynamic pricing and ads in the face of perfectly rational agents, raises prices for consumers and takes a bigger cut from manufacturers. “Generally, if one fee goes away, you get another,” Fradkin said. In other words, everything could be faster, easier, and more efficient for the consumer—but potentially more expensive. Van Loo said that the bigger AI companies will eventually find ways to strike deals with platforms via these protocols, negotiating access, commissions, and partnerships in ways that benefit the companies, not necessarily the consumers. This could result in a sort of preferential treatment like the deals already in place between Meta and Walmart, Sephora, and other retailers, which will effectively cause Muse to prioritize their products. Taking another approach, Amazon has blocked Muse and encourages visitors to browse with its own agent, “Alexa for Shopping,” meaning the company is basically negotiating on both sides of the deal. Meanwhile, this week, JPMorgan announced that it would not allow Instinct, Muse, or other agents into customer accounts. Ultimately, this might all lead to “the same old heavily obstructed, inefficient world we have now,” Van Loo said. “But it will look far more efficient, because it will save some people time and feel much more convenient.” Very powerful companies will design new structures for markets and the internet, determining what can be sold, by whom, and for how much—as they always have. For all the time and money the agentic future could save us, the technology entails another sort of cost: an additional layer of abstraction and disengagement. We’ve largely outsourced our decision making to a small number of platforms: Amazon guides our shopping; Google Maps steers us toward certain restaurants and primary-care providers; Instagram dictates our news consumption. We are told that these recommendations and ads are, based on troves of personal data, already optimal. The companies pushing agents assure us that the decision making will now be even more rational and the deals even better. But checking these claims for ourselves will be harder, because the logic behind those recommendations will be buried in large-language-model chains of reasoning. Eventually, the skeptical instinct to check agents’ work could atrophy altogether. Over time, humans will play a smaller and smaller role in their own life. In the age of the algorithm, it’s easy to throw out cliché terms such as late-stage capitalism in an attempt to describe the extractive, inhumane dynamics of the economy. But what is an agentic future if not the furthest extension of our current market logic? A future of capitalism so perfect, so efficient, that it doesn’t need us at all.

items.title: Quatre interpellations et une importante saisie de cannabis dans deux opérations antidrogue
items.description: Trois individus ont été interpellés à Korhogo, en Côte d'Ivoire, pour «détention illicite» et vente de cannabis et de comprimés de Tramadol, tandis qu’un autre a été arrêté à Guiglo avec cinq kilogrammes de cannabis. Ces interventions, menées dans le cadre de l’opération «Épervier Spécial», ont permis aux forces de police ivoiriennes de saisir plusieurs produits stupéfiants. La lutte contre le trafic de drogue se poursuit en Côte d’Ivoire. Le Groupe de répression anti-drogue (GRAD) a mené deux interventions distinctes à Korhogo et à Guiglo, aboutissant à l’interpellation de quatre individus et à la saisie de cannabis ainsi que de comprimés de Tramadol. Selon une note de la Direction générale de la Police nationale de Côte d’Ivoire (DGPN), publiée le jeudi 15 octobre 2026, la première opération s’est déroulée le mercredi 14 octobre à Korhogo, dans le nord du pays. Elle faisait suite à des renseignements signalant l’existence d’un point de vente de cannabis dans un bas-fond situé entre les quartiers Sinistré et Soba. Pour vérifier ces informations et procéder à d’éventuelles interpellations, trois équipages du GRAD ont été déployés sur les lieux. L’intervention a permis d’interpeller en flagrant délit trois individus identifiés par les initiales Y.F.J., âgé de 20 ans, S.G.A. et C.Z.A., tous deux âgés de 19 ans. La fouille des lieux et des suspects a conduit à la découverte de cinq blocs de cannabis, de deux ballons de cannabis de type «OG-KUSH», de 16 pochons de la même variété et de 11 comprimés de Tramadol dosés à 250 mg. Une seconde intervention a été menée par le GRAD dans la localité de V16, à Guiglo, dans le cadre d’une opération de recherche et de destruction de fumoirs. Elle a abouti à l’interpellation d’un homme âgé de 34 ans et à la saisie de cinq kilogrammes de cannabis. Ces deux opérations s’inscrivent dans le cadre de l’opération «Épervier Spécial», mise en œuvre pour lutter contre le trafic et la circulation des stupéfiants. Elles illustrent la poursuite des actions de la Police nationale ivoirienne contre les réseaux de distribution de drogues et les lieux servant à leur consommation. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Quatre interpellations et une importante saisie de cannabis dans deux opérations antidrogue est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Dialogue social : le Premier ministre Ahmadou Alhaminou LO demande un moratoire de trois mois sur les grèves
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO, a appelé les partenaires sociaux à privilégier la concertation et annoncé la mise en place, dès décembre 2026, de comités de dialogue social dans tous les ministères. Cette démarche intervient alors que le suivi du Pacte national de stabilité sociale fait état d’un taux de réalisation de 71 % des engagements des parties. Le Premier ministre, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO, a demandé aux organisations syndicales d’observer un moratoire de trois mois sur les grèves annoncées, tout en réaffirmant la volonté de l’État de respecter ses engagements. Il s’exprimait jeudi 15 octobre 2026, au Building administratif Président Mamadou DIA, lors d’une réunion du Comité de pilotage tripartite du Pacte national de stabilité sociale pour une croissance inclusive et durable. La rencontre a réuni des membres du Gouvernement, des représentants du patronat et des organisations syndicales autour de l’état d’avancement des engagements pris dans le cadre de ce pacte. Selon le dispositif de suivi-évaluation présenté à cette occasion, le taux de réalisation des engagements du Gouvernement et des partenaires sociaux s’établit à 71 %. Face aux tensions sociales, le chef du Gouvernement a invité les différentes parties à privilégier le dialogue afin de parvenir à des solutions concertées. Il a assuré que les engagements de l’État seraient scrupuleusement respectés, en tenant compte du rétablissement des moyens nécessaires à leur mise en œuvre. Le Premier ministre a également demandé aux syndicats de privilégier la concertation plutôt que le recours à une grève générale, en proposant un moratoire de trois mois pour donner davantage de temps aux discussions et à la recherche de solutions. Pour renforcer ce dispositif, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO a annoncé la mise en place, dès décembre 2026, de comités de dialogue social dans l’ensemble des ministères. Cette mesure vise à consolider les mécanismes de concertation entre l’administration et les partenaires sociaux et à favoriser le règlement des différends en amont. Ces annonces s’inscrivent dans la mise en œuvre du Pacte national de stabilité sociale pour une croissance inclusive et durable, qui repose sur l’engagement des pouvoirs publics, des organisations syndicales et du patronat à promouvoir un climat social apaisé. Le taux de réalisation de 71 % constitue un indicateur de l’état d’avancement des engagements pris. La poursuite du dialogue et la concrétisation des mesures restantes demeurent des enjeux importants pour consolider la confiance entre les différentes parties et prévenir de nouvelles tensions sociales.

items.title: What Three Gene-Therapy Deaths Have in Common
items.description: In recent months, news came out about several distressing cases that have underscored the risks of gene therapy, which delivers DNA to a patient’s cells to treat disease. All of these cases have one thing in common that’s not apparent at first glance. A child in China , enrolled in a clinical trial for gene therapy, died of acute respiratory distress syndrome, in which fluid builds up in the lungs and oxygen cannot enter. In a separate clinical trial in China, a child died after clots formed in their small blood vessels, likely disrupting the delivery of oxygen to organs such as the kidneys and brain. And earlier this year, researchers reported that a 5-year-old boy treated in Philadelphia had a brain tumor that was likely caused by gene therapy. (He’s doing okay now.) In each of these cases, the gene therapies relied on a versatile but unpredictable type of virus: adeno-associated virus, or AAV for short. AAVs are the workhorses of many of the most successful gene therapies in the world. Scientists modify them so that they can deliver a working copy of particular genes to the body, but cannot replicate and aren’t infectious. These treatments have transformed a form of spinal muscular atrophy—once the genetic disorder most responsible for infant mortality—into a survivable condition, and have been approved for a devastating enzyme deficiency, muscle-wasting disease, and hemophilia, to name a few. The terrible outcomes AAVs can cause are rare, but they’re a real risk. So far, the treatments have been used in small patient groups—the most commonly given one has been received by about 5,000 children since 2019—and focused on diseases that dramatically affect or shorten people’s lives. But AAV-based gene therapies are being explored for prevalent ailments, including heart disease, high blood pressure, and perhaps even Alzheimer’s. As the use of gene therapy increases, so might the instances in which it goes dramatically wrong. The modified AAVs involved in gene therapy each contain a single strand of DNA. One portion of that strand drives the virus’s ability to get inside cells, and another is the helpful human gene that’s being delivered. The viral components are more likely than the therapeutic gene to be unpredictable and can cause side effects. On occasion, for instance, instead of hanging around within cells, AAVs insert themselves into the patient’s genetic code. This seems to have been what happened to the 5-year-old who developed a brain tumor—the AAV put itself into a part of his DNA that then produced the cancer. Hurler syndrome, the condition the boy was being treated for when he received the gene therapy at 13 months old, is progressively debilitating. The syndrome can cause problems for the skeleton, heart, lungs, and liver, and affect cognitive development; life expectancy is short. Many gene therapies are geared toward children for whom a working copy of a vital gene would promise something closer to a healthy life. “We should remember what diseases we are talking about,” Albert Rizvanov, a scientist at Kazan Federal University in Russia who studies gene therapy, told me. For such patients, gene therapy may seem like an obvious choice. But parents are still left weighing the potential benefits of treatment against the real risks, including fatal complications. Jo Kaur and her husband, Richie DiGeorge, faced this question not too long ago. Their son Riaan was born in 2019 weighing less than six pounds, and by the time he was three months of age, they were concerned about his eyesight. Riaan’s pediatrician suspected it was just near-sightedness, Kaur, who has written extensively online about her family’s story, told me, but her “mom radar went off.” She secured an appointment with an ophthalmologist who found that her son had cataracts in both his eyes. Riaan’s overall growth also wasn’t on track, and he was missing milestones. At 15 months old, he was diagnosed with a severe form of Cockayne syndrome, a genetic condition that causes progressive muscle weakness and nerve damage. This diagnosis meant not just that Riaan had problems with his eyes or was growing a little slowly, but that his life would likely be short—perhaps just five to seven years. He could roll and pull his family in for cuddles, but by the time he was 6 years old, at the end of 2025, he was still unable to sit independently for more than a few minutes at a time, or stand or walk independently, or feed himself. He was so small that he was still wearing clothes for 18-month-olds. By then, Riaan had lost a lot of nervous tissue. His brain size was about 50 percent of what would be typical for a child his age. But Kaur and DiGeorge had worked closely with scientists for years to develop a gene therapy for Cockayne syndrome. The hope was to stop or at least slow Riaan’s loss of nerve cells. “Because Cockayne syndrome is neurodegenerative, even an extended period in which Riaan simply remains where he is now would be enormously meaningful to us,” Kaur said. The researchers developing a Cockayne-syndrome treatment for Riaan had done mouse experiments to determine whether the medication was safe and whether it worked. Some of the animals had signs of liver damage, but they also lived longer. Kaur and her husband had been involved in countless meetings and stayed up-to-date on all of the developments. Knowing the risks so intimately increased the weight of the decision to allow Riaan to receive the treatment. “We’d read all the papers, we knew the science,” she said, “but you’re still making a huge decision for your child.” She and her husband were primarily concerned about the treatment’s safety. Ultimately, this past April, they decided to go ahead with the therapy. Riaan would be the first child in the world to receive this treatment for Cockayne syndrome. Surgeons created a small hole in his skull, inserted a catheter, and within minutes delivered the gene therapy to him. When night came, as Kaur wrote in her own account of Riaan’s procedure, she fought the urge to sneeze as he slept on her arm in the hospital. Everything seemed very delicate, and she dared not move. His head had to stay elevated and he “had so many wires,” she told me. “I didn’t want to wake him.” The first successful gene therapy, tested back in 1990, used a nonreplicating version of a mouse virus. But that virus doesn’t readily get into all cells, so scientists kept looking for others to try. One was adenovirus—an attractive option in part because it could deliver working genes to a high number of cells. But in 1999, an 18-year-old named Jesse Gelsinger died shortly after having a severe immunological response to a therapy that used adenovirus to treat his rare metabolic disorder. Gelsinger is believed to have experienced the same acute respiratory distress syndrome that killed one of the patients in China. In that recent trial, the Chinese company HuidaGene Therapeutics was using gene therapy to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy. In many cases, the body weakness caused by Duchenne leads to death during a child’s teenage years, and families whose kids might benefit from gene therapy have been pushing for it. In the United States, a different AAV-based gene-therapy treatment for Duchenne, made by the company Sarepta, has been controversial in part because of concerns that it may not actually do enough for patients. But it has also been associated with deaths: Last summer, the FDA reported that it was investigating after several patients receiving Sarepta’s therapy succumbed to acute liver failure, a known risk. (After the deaths, in a public statement, HuidaGene extended condolences to the family and reiterated its focus on patient safety. Sarepta paused shipments of treatment for certain patients.) AAVs delivered into the bloodstream are very good at reaching the liver, where they’re filtered out and can accumulate. As a result, the engineered viruses can have a harder time reaching other organ systems and tissues, including muscle. To get to those harder-to-reach parts of the body, sometimes scientists increase the amount of treatment they give. The doses of viral particles in gene therapy can vary so widely that one type of treatment might have a dose of 500 billion functional viral particles per kilogram, and another 300 trillion. (The doses in commonly used drugs tend to occupy a much narrower range.) Many patients have few other options than to risk a bigger dose, Luk Vandenberghe, who was involved in the discovery of a commonly used AAV and now directs the gene-therapy center at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary, told me. “The alternatives can mean restarting development with a new and modified gene therapy,” he said. Researchers have been trying to test different variants of AAV and engineering the viruses’ shells to get them to reach desired tissues in the body. But that, too, can change how the body reacts. A year ago, a child died in a clinical trial that used an AAV designed with a shell to help it reach the brain and deliver treatment for a congenital seizure disorder. The company behind the trial, Capsida, paused the clinical trial and a few months later said that the child had experienced brain swelling following the infusion. In May, it announced that it had closed the trial. (The company has “been conducting extensive nonclinical work to understand what led to the outcome” and will incorporate its findings into future work, Katherine Carlyle Smith, a Capsida spokesperson, wrote in an email.) Despite the risks of gene therapy, the growing number of people who have received it also means that many people have benefited, without concerning side effects. “Caution is of course always top of mind, but I think the promise of gene therapy overwhelms the risks of not taking action for a lot of parents,” Kaur, Riaan’s mother, told me. She and her husband felt especially cautious about giving Riaan gene therapy, precisely because he had a life-limiting disease: “We want to maintain and preserve the life and happiness that he currently has,” she said. Currently, Riaan is being tapered off his immunosuppressants and monitored closely. In the meantime, Kaur is observing signs that the therapy might be helping. He can sit by himself on the edge of the couch. He still needs support to stand or walk, but he wants to try more often. Kaur knows these observations are anecdotal, but Riaan’s physical therapist has also noticed the changes, she said. He has become more expressive, too—an outcome that surprised Kaur. “He would rarely say ‘mama,’ and now he says it all day long … ‘ma-ma-ma,’” she says. “It’s beautiful to hear.”

items.title: The Cutest Target of Trump’s D.C. Makeover
items.description: When Donald Trump flies over Washington’s East Potomac Park, as he does on his helicopter rides to Joint Base Andrews, he sees a piece of prime waterfront real estate with serious PGA potential . In what might as well be another episode of Extreme Makeover: Capital Edition , the president wants to convert the more than 300-acre man-made island and its affordable golf course into a championship-worthy destination. But it turns out that there’s a lot you can’t perceive from the sky. The park, which Trump visited for 90 minutes in June, buzzes with life. Municipal golfers—hardly the country-club set—trek across the green. Cyclists and runners collect miles on Ohio Drive, the road that circles the wing-shaped island. Fishers and picnickers sit along Hains Point, the park’s tip. Many locals fear that they could lose all of this if the president gets his golf-course glow-up. Although it sits just south of Washington’s expanse of monuments, East Potomac Park isn’t typically a site of controversy. Usually, its biggest moment comes each spring, when its cherry trees blossom. But the attention was less cheerful on Saturday, when the National Park Service went on a sudden tree-chopping spree. The agency cut down more than 400 trees along the course, prompting worries that it might be using maintenance as a cover for beginning work on Trump’s grander plans, which still face bureaucratic hurdles. On Monday, timber was piled up on the golf course. Among the standing trees, I counted about 75 marked with caution tape to save them from the axe. A lone protester held a sign that read Stop Tree Genocide . Ana C. Reyes, the federal judge presiding over a lawsuit about the renovation, lambasted the administration in an emergency court hearing that day, saying that officials had lost all credibility in the case. She has since extended an order to stop the government from clearing trees through October 26 and is requiring the administration to provide three business days’ notice before it makes irreparable changes to the golf course. A lawyer for the government told Reyes that officials had done their best to notify her of their plans ahead of time, as she’d requested. “No, you did not do your best,” Reyes said. “You did your absolute worst.” Few know what will happen to East Potomac Park if Trump gets his way. Full plans for the golf-course project have not been released, and the National Park Service canceled a historic-preservation meeting, which might have offered the public some insight. (The park is on the National Register of Historic Places and is subject to extensive review.) But Trump has given indications that this public park might soon take on a more exclusive air. For many, last year’s sudden East Wing demolition destroyed a symbol of the American people. The plans for East Potomac Park represent something far more tangible; people feel that the White House is trying to seize part of their neighborhood. There’s another, even lesser-known corner of East Potomac Park. Hidden beneath a canopy of trees lies the cutest potential casualty of the renovation projects that have occupied much of Trump’s time during his second term: the country’s oldest continually running mini-golf course. (There are competing claims to that superlative.) It’s a microcosm of a microcosm—the most welcoming place in a park made, by congressional act, for the public. Eric Lee for The Atlantic / Eric Lee Perhaps the reelection of a golf-loving, resort-owning president was always going to affect the three low-cost municipal golf courses in Washington, D.C., which are on land controlled by the National Park Service. Last December, the Trump administration suddenly terminated a nonprofit’s leases to operate the sites. That group, National Links Trust, made a deal with the White House in May to continue running two of the courses long-term and East Potomac Golf Links in the interim, before its White House–led renovation. The president tapped the well-known golf architect Tom Fazio, a longtime collaborator who has worked on a handful of Trump courses, to run the project. Trump criticized the site as “dilapidated, worn out, and very dangerous and outdated” and vowed to turn it into a host site for major tournaments. Creating such a course would likely require taking over almost the whole park. The Washington Post reported last month that Trump has been fixated on eliminating Ohio Drive and extending the course to the island’s edge, a change that could make jogging or cycling around the park impossible. In response to questions about the project, a White House spokesperson told me that Trump would restore its “glamour and prestige,” writing, “As a private citizen, President Trump built some of the greatest golf courses in the world, and he is now extending his unmatched design skills and excellent eye for detail to D.C.’s East Potomac Golf Links.” The Department of the Interior told me that “DOI and NPS are committed to continuing the relationships we have built with the local golf communities to ensure these courses are safe, beautiful, open, affordable, enjoyable, accessible, and world-class for people living in and visiting the greatest capital city in the world.” DOI did not respond when asked a second time about whether the mini-golf course will remain. The attraction did not seem to be included in renderings of the course disseminated by the National Garden of American Heroes Foundation, a Trump-associated fundraising entity. Nor was mini-golf visible on a design of the new course that Trump was photographed holding during his summer tour. Eric Lee for The Atlantic / Eric Lee This may seem like a small problem—mini, even. But the humble course speaks to the broader dismissiveness toward D.C. residents that has characterized Trump’s impositions on the capital. The changes can be felt across the city: the year-plus deployment of National Guard troops on neighborhood streets; the fencing-off of public spaces such as Lafayette Square; the takeover of the Kennedy Center, which has been all but shut down. Municipal golf courses, which are owned or operated by local governments, are known for widening access to a sport associated with the wealthy. Nowhere is this democratic spirit more alive than on a municipal mini-golf course frequented by children, parents, and newbies to the green. Somehow, on my first round of the fun-size sport in more than a decade, I hit a hole in one. I played the mini-golf course this spring with Ryan Moody, a landscape architect who’d worked on a 2024 renovation of the mini course, and Michael McCartin, a co-founder of National Links Trust. As we strolled past the classical-columned clubhouse, Moody mentioned that he was planning to host his son’s fifth-birthday party there; McCartin said that he was pretty sure he’d had his own tenth birthday at the mini-golf course, decades ago. [ Read: The capital is a mess ] The mini course has a retro feel and a simple design that should not be mistaken for technical simplicity. It might be the toughest mini-golf course in the country, McCartin warned. There’s no rating system, he clarified, but whereas newer mini-golf courses are dominated by easier holes, this one is full of elaborate, multistep excursions. Nearly 100 years old, it is blissfully uninterested in granting players instant gratification. Mini-golf conjures images of theme-park kitsch—faux volcanos, towering plastic dinosaurs. With its clean lines, concrete edges, stone walls, and limited color palette, the East Potomac mini-golf course is closer to bureaucracy-core. It has some decorative touches: a loop-de-loop here and a wishing well there, but overall, the atmosphere is understated. You’re supposed to feel like you’re golfing in a garden, Moody told me. As actual golfers took their shots on the larger courses around us, McCartin coached us. At one point, I thought I’d hit another hole in one, but then I discovered that the ball had gone through a hidden tunnel and ended up on another green with even more steps to the actual finish. On another hole, I simply gave up counting my attempts, which were well into the double digits. One hole involved hitting the ball through replicas of nearby landmarks. (You could imagine the addition of a triumphal arch if the course survives.) When I accidentally overshot a ball and it flew over the White House, the U.S. Capitol, and Mount Vernon, my golfing partners let me keep going from where it landed. Jumping over governmental obstacles felt like some kind of metaphor. Eric Lee for The Atlantic / Eric Lee Remote and central at the same time, East Potomac Park provides an escape from city life. Congress designated the site in 1897 “to be forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people.” Alex Rosen, a D.C. resident who recently founded Save East Po, an activist group opposing Trump’s renovation, told me that every addition to the park, such as the cherry trees and Ohio Drive, “has broadened and expanded what it means to have recreation on this peninsula.” The 18-hole mini-golf course opened during the Great Depression and became among the park’s most popular sites. When Moody took on its revamp, the tiny course was in disrepair, but he studied old photos and tried to bring past elements back, such as catenary lighting that once kept the place open late. “It’s respectful of the historic layout of the course,” he said, a layout that has “stood the test of time.” In contrast, the plan for a professional-grade course risks sharing a heavy-handed quality with Trump’s other D.C. projects. Ideas like the triumphal arch are “all sort of plopped down in the landscape, aggressively and without any recognition of continuity of visual and spatial relationships,” Charles Birnbaum, a landscape architect who leads the Cultural Landscape Foundation, a group that has opposed many of Trump’s changes, told me. The mini-golf course may have continuity with the landscape, but if I’m being honest, it does not have continuity with how I like to spend an afternoon. If I could save one feature of East Potomac Park from Trump’s wrecking ball, it would not be the mini. Ohio Drive has my vote. But that’s the beauty of the place. I’m not forcing the golfers to join me on my 10-mile run, and I don’t need to join them with my 10-over-par. In a world where East Potomac Park is doing what Congress intended, no activity needs to be sacrificed for anyone else’s favorite sport.

items.title: Maurice: les habitants de Goodlands entre condamnation des violences et colère contre le gouvernement
items.description: Le retour au calme reste fragile à Maurice après deux nuits de tensions et de violences liées notamment aux problèmes de distribution d’eau et au tir d’un policier sur un véhicule, qui a grièvement blessé en début de semaine une jeune femme de 29 ans rentrant du travail. Le gouvernement a instauré un couvre-feu nocturne, dont la troisième nuit s’achève ce vendredi matin. À Goodlands, dans le nord de l’île, les habitants oscillent entre condamnation des débordements et colère contre le gouvernement.

items.title: ‘Revolution, the dirty word’: On Lara Baladi’s Z for Zarafa
items.description: What happens after revolution? How do we remember, if we do at all? In her exhibition, Z for Zarafa, which opened at Gypsum Gallery at the start of June and closed on September 23, Lara Baladi takes us through a scavenger hunt of moments, leading us into an archive of revolution, specifically looked at from an aftermath vantage point of movement, migration, displacement and the ultimate wrestling for freedom. The exhibition acts as a physical installation of aspects of an online database, Anatomy of Revolution , which is a project exploring the various iconography and language of resistance movements. The database consolidates research, visual, written and audio material from past and present global struggles, which Baladi gathered between 2011 and 2021 as part of her project, Vox Populi, Tahrir Archives . The body of data, a vast space of references, is organized into an abecedary using the Arabic alphabet, designed to work as “an educational primer of struggles for freedom.” The exhibition, a multi-year effort through a wide network of collaborations, brought together the works of editors, writers and visual artists reflecting on experiences of migration and exile, alongside the works of refugee women in Cairo, blacksmiths in Imbaba, antiquaries in downtown Cairo, embroiderers in Islamic Cairo and potters in Fayoum, among others. The opening day marked the launch of the first edition of The Anatomist, a publication “befriending” themes of “displacement, borders, exile and return” through commissioned articles and testimonies, a “companion” to the exhibition. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. In the website abecedary, if we jump to the letter Z, we find the story of a giraffe named Zarafa, a diplomatic gift sent from Mohamed Ali Pasha to King Charles X in 1826. She was captured by hunters in Sennar, Sudan before being taken to France. Destined for a life of spectacle, she, along with her handler Hassan al-Berbery, made the arduous journey to Paris, crossing the sea through Alexandria and Marseille, to satisfy a cosmetic political urge: first by camel, then aboard a felucca, before embarking a ship and then completing a 900 km journey on foot. Once in Marseille, she had to be hidden out of fear of her premature discovery, so the walk to Paris was completed at night with her head and eyes covered. It took 32 days. She would be the first giraffe in France. Once Zarafa arrived at the destination at the Jardins des Plantes in Paris, she sparked a cultural and fashion frenzy. People would line up to see her, feed her petals, celebrate her, even dress like her. She lived the rest of her life for the next 18 years confined in the beautiful yet estranging garden, available to the public for entertainment. “ Forced out of her home in Sudan and into an estranged existence in France ,” Zarafa, or Zoo-Zoo as her handler would call her, becomes a metaphor for migration. The story and image of Zarafa and how it generated a cultural frenzy are our entry point to the exhibition, capturing the transformation, or recognition, of an image becoming a symbol that garners a collective shared meaning and response. This shift in meaning is examined through the exhibition’s main reflection on migration and return; we start to explore stories of movement and the political and personal dimensions of cultural exchange before the physical experience takes us through historical, present and personal stories of migration and displacement. These confounded layers of movement, exchange, migration and displacement lead us into a portal to Baladi’s data on struggles for freedom, of which Zarafa is an excerpt. At the exhibition’s entrance, we are faced with For Glory of the Wind and Water, a tapestry holding moments woven through fabric, depicting tragedies which have seared through minds and into the public consciousness, like the viral image of Aylan Kurdi, the three-year-old Syrian toddler who was found dead on a Turkish beach in 2015. He, his five-year-old brother and their mother drowned in the Mediterranean minutes into the dangerous journey of trying to escape from Syria to Greece. In the tapestry, we also see images selected by Baladi, like Dorothea Lange’s Migrant Mother , a photo which became a global symbol of the Great Depression, taken in 1936 of a farmworker and her children at a pea picker camp in California. Zarafa appears in the tapestry in illustrations of her travels by boat and her arrival to France. Beside these images, stories of marginalized refugee women are woven into the fabric, following a series of workshops with them, led by Baladi and organized in collaboration with nongovernmental organization Threads of Hope. Scenes of protest are also seen in the tapestry. With all of these elements, the tapestry becomes a collage of documented experiences, taking the audience through multiple stories at once. It introduces a simultaneity in how we engage with themes of struggle, movement and belonging. The tactility in the tapestry reflects Baladi’s insistence on tangibility. Although the database is online, the tangible component is important. “The tangible provides an extraordinary possibility of collaborating,” Baladi says during a talk held in Diwan Bookstore on September 8, describing her attachment to sourcing materials and working with artists to produce physical installations. In the same room, there are several photographs. One of them delivers a sharp sense of doom; it’s an image of a black sea, its waves foaming, captured at night time. The rawness of the photo contrasts with the tapestry depictions, which, while still real, are more narrativized, delivering known stories and experiences the public has been exposed to in ways that try to make them comprehensible. Whereas in this photo, there is a harshness of the unknown you encounter; you are left to imagine the potential stories and experiences it holds, the different realities. It cuts through the frame and immediately into your brain. It is daunting. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. In The Anatomist, the publication launched in tandem with the exhibition as another layer of navigation that Baladi and her team propose, Rafaelle Bertault describes her experience as a migration caseworker conducting interviews and the day she decided to quit. One day, six years into working this job, she met a man with severe post-traumatic stress disorder whose friend had drowned after they tried to escape on a smuggling boat from Turkey that capsized. “He started crying and blaming himself for his death. I broke down and cried too. And so did the interpreter.” Describing it as a tipping point in the text titled Shipwreck, she writes that she was angry that all of this could have been prevented. Bertault had the same reaction six years later, in June 2023, to the news of one of the deadliest migrant disasters in history, the capsizing of the Adriana, a boat carrying 750 undocumented migrants from Libya which sank in Greek waters. Only 103 passengers survived, and the bodies of 82 people were recovered. “When I heard the journalist ask the sea-rescue activists whether the ‘migrants should have been saved’ (and it is a legal obligation to do so), I screamed,” she writes. A week later, “a French submarine was chartered at great expense to search for the five presumed dead billionaires who had each spent $25,000 to visit the site of the Titanic’s wreck. Here the journalists asked whether the rich men could be saved.” It was revealed last year that the Greek coastguard was aware of the boat in distress and chose not to intervene in the 12 hours before it capsized. Also in the publication, Jonathan Hearn reflects on the feeling of losing one’s sense of place as he describes Edge of Place, a painting by Radfan al-Mohammadi. The artwork Hearn is referring to was in response to the outbreak of the Yemeni civil war in 2014 and was produced when Mohammadi moved from Yemen to Egypt in 2016. Hearn describes meeting Mohammadi in 2023 at the Cairo Opera House where the artist explained that the girl’s glistening eyes in the artwork reflect the imagined future of the Yemeni anti-regime protesters of 2011. “Like al-Mohammadi, these men and women believed their political movement would build a better country. Yet, instead of entering that promised land, many now wrestle with the thought that they have given up home. Even if fragile and threatened, a known home may be worth more than a home that is only a mirage,” Hearn writes. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Before we get to the second and final room of the exhibition, we walk through a corridor that Baladi made sure to activate. It was important for her to use the space as a way to “keep people in the work so they don’t run away or escape from it,” she says, describing the refuge an empty corridor can sometimes offer. Along the corridor, there are framed posters of text, including, for example, “WE ARE AS IT WERE STRANGERS TO OURSELVES.” The placement aims to reflect the migratory nature of existentialism, Baladi says, an internal process always in movement. There is also a poster with the text, “I AM MAN,” a visual reference of the 1968 Memphis sanitation workers strike in which more than 1300 Black sanitation workers marched through the streets to protest their dehumanization. When photographs of the strikes were published, the words and images captured became a global symbol for the demand for human dignity, the constituent of which is the simple statement of I AM MAN. The second room is presented as a classroom, complete with a student desk and a wall featuring the letters of the Arabic alphabet. Each of the 28 letters is accompanied by an image and a word: ب for بلد ( balad ), ت for تاريخ ( tareekh ), ث for ثورة ( thawra ), ح for حرية ( horreya ), خ for خبز ( khobz ). Country, history, revolution, freedom, bread. To the opposite wall, there is a framed poster, The Wheel, a collage bursting with revolution iconography, sourced from the internet, arranged in the shape of a circle, with what appears to be blood splattered along the top frame. And in between those two walls, a screen is installed on a chalkboard wall, playing a video introducing us to the online archive, Anatomy of Revolution. The classroom points to pedagogy as a playful mechanism in the exhibition, one which Baladi imbues with her own references, including from the online archive. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Returning to the point of entry, adjacent to the For the Glory of the Wind and Water tapestry, a quote from French philosopher Gilles Deleuze is arranged on the wall in the shape of a zigzag. “Z is for zig zag. The fly, the zed of the fly, the zigging movements of the fly, the Zed. It is the final word. There is no word after zigzag. […] It is perhaps the elementary movement, Z as movement, the fly…perhaps the movement that presided at the creation of the world.” Deleuze is also featured in The Anatomist’s How to Read a Dictionary According to Deleuze. In the text, Farida Youssef, who co-edited the publication with Baladi, argues for Deleuze’s Z for zigzag concept in reading a dictionary: to reorient our ways of thinking by moving from the traditional approach of reading from cover to cover, in a way in which the rigid, linear sequence of the alphabet determines the order of comprehension, a predetermined structure set in stone, and to instead navigate such a book like a zigzag, in an agile practice offering other possibilities for the development of ideas, linkages and potentials. This turns reading into a dynamic, physical process of concept creation, of flying in a zigzag from place to place to trace connections and form knowledge. “If you start with ‘c for colonialism’ and then read ‘w for war’ before ending with ‘m for migration,’ you will probably understand the concept of ‘i for injustice’,” Youssef writes. In the exhibition, the placement and dispersal of the items throughout the room, whether on the wall, in a frame, on a table, and their relation to one another forces the navigating viewer, as well as their attention, into an anatomical movement, reminiscent of the zigzag, a disruptive, disorienting but logical interruption to a traditional, simpler or predetermined flow. The same applies in terms of the exhibition’s other modes to navigate, the publication and website, and in how they relate to each other as well as to the other physical elements, engaging the participant into a referential dance of a similar nature. The choice of the words of Deleuze and the figures of the zigzag are suited to the aspiration behind the publication. In L’Abécédaire de Gilles Deleuze , a series of interviews published posthumously, Deleuze explains to journalist Claire Parnet his theory on the zigzag. “It’s the Zed of bifurcation, of lightning,” he tells her, “and a great letter that establishes a return to A.” Speaking in terms of physics , he discusses how to bring divergent singularities, or different potentials, into relation with one another. According to him, a phenomenon occurs between two potentials through a “somber precursor.” Once that precursor situation begins, the potentials are left in a state of reaction, from which a visible event emerges. “So, there is the somber precursor and then a lightning bolt, and that’s how the world was born. There is always a somber precursor that no one sees and then the lightning bolt that illuminates, and there is the world,” he says. Baladi refers to the zigzag as a methodology for the exhibition. No one can dispute the sight of a bolt of lightning. It is undeniable. The exhibition is a collation and exploration of these bolts and the moments which preceded them, the somber precursors that have led to a certain state of reaction. Seen in this light, the bolts engage a piercing public and intimate understanding of a struggle for freedom, an undeniable recognition of what became a symbol, born out of this zap of conception. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. But what happens when this mode of navigation is presented to a public to whom symbols are to be interpreted and connections to be made, as individuals and, also, collectively? Aside from the works on exhibit, the written work, which steers interpretation into a discourse, the website and the overall philosophy of the zigzag, there is much left in the hands of the audience. They exist as participants in the practice of protecting and engaging with knowledge and, specifically, the visual identities of history, by seeking to understand or collectively remember what is being displayed. The exhibition, with the website as its umbrella, asks us to reflect on images and symbols that have garnered a mass social response at a certain time. For example, if we scroll down to “ت” or “Ta,” we find an entry for torture. Among the data compiled in the section, there are images from the Iranian Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, which was triggered by the killing of Mahsa Amini after she was arrested by Iranian morality police in 2022. Below the social media artwork, there is a collage of the mugshots of women who were tortured at the Towhid Prison, run by Iran’s pre-revolution intelligence service, SAVAK, which was overseen by the shah from 1957-1979, accompanied by a quote: “Torture still scars Iranians 40 years after revolution,” originally published in The San Francisco Chronicle by Nasser Karimi and Job Gambrell. Both are installed at the prison’s premises in Tehran, which now operates instead as the Ebrat museum of torture. When asked about the shift in the exhibition’s modes of viewing, its intention to traverse from individual to the collective, the personal and the public, one visitor speaks of the fragmentary air of the project that, in a way, dismantles collective experiences into moments, fragments and details, summoning a different kind of attention than what is wielded when remembering something collectively. “It’s like the exhibition dismantles the public of revolution, alongside revolution itself, breaking their wholeness open, maybe for a possible re-arrangement or just running with one of the fragments. It’s an interesting license the artist and the art take for themselves. It’s almost a license to disorient us, despite the dictionary, the database and all these pedagogic gestures. And we aren’t disoriented together. We are disoriented alone, facing what is being done to a memory once collective. The only collective experience is that we are just a bunch of merry exhibition goers and art consumers,” they say. In Baladi’s own narrative, voiced during the September talk in Diwan, she responds on the relation: “Revolution, the dirty word. … This is not about revolution. It’s about what happens after.” Her question is, ultimately, how art addresses revolution. It is about how symbols are taken, used, interpreted and reinterpreted, or reformed, she says. The above visitor wonders, “What does this intention make of art?” Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. The journey of Zarafa is a promise of a life unrealized, masked under the cover of diplomacy. Baladi was initiating the Anatomy of Revolution project in 2019 when she added Zarafa’s story, with a quest to investigate questions of cultural exchange. This shows up elsewhere in the exhibition. In the middle of the first room, we see a stuffed panda sitting in a transparent box, a reference to Chinese Panda diplomacy, when China used to offer pandas as diplomatic gifts until the practice was stopped in the 1980s. The panda has its back to the corridor which leads to the classroom part of the exhibition. In the same room, there are also references of diplomatic exchange and political persuasion, including a “cabinet of curiosities” with objects referring to ceremonial gifts exchanged between state heads, as well as ceramic objects displayed on tables referencing pharaonic medallions, a symbol for military achievement. In migration, a physical and psychological process, surviving is for the lucky ones. But in being granted the privilege of continuation, what does life look like then? Is it a life of our choosing? Or are we captive, physically, psychologically, to the limits constricting us, which, if we’re not careful, will determine how we think, what we think or if we even think at all? What we risk is having a pacifying but fake, implanted, shared meaning, engineering a collective identity designed to produce a mechanical mass social behavior and response. All of this has led me to thinking of revolution as a journey distorted, one archived in life, deformed or buried alive, in most cases; prematurely fossilized, or captured, and frozen in time. And so, Zarafa’s life, maybe, is also a metaphor for revolution. A story holding the painful movement to another place for the promise of a certain freedom, driven and shaped by politics. And we are left to think about what happens when we arrive, post-movement. What becomes of the memory, and how do we remember? The post ‘Revolution, the dirty word’: On Lara Baladi’s Z for Zarafa first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus : AGEROUTE Guinée mise sur la sensibilisation pour sauver des vies
items.description: Face aux ravages du cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus, AGEROUTE Guinée fait de la sensibilisation un levier de prévention et de protection de la santé des femmes. A travers une séance d’information animée par des spécialistes en gynécologie-obstétrique, les travailleurs de l’institution ont été édifiés sur les causes, les signes d’alerte, l’importance du dépistage précoce et les conséquences d’une prise en charge tardive. Une initiative qui a suscité une prise de conscience et fait naître un engagement collectif : relayer l’information pour sauver des vies. Briser le silence, lever les tabous et encourager les femmes à se faire dépister, c’est le message fort qui a marqué la séance de sensibilisation organisée par l’Agence de gestion des routes de Guinée (AGEROUTE Guinée) autour du cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus. Dans une société où le manque d’information, la gêne et la peur peuvent encore retarder le recours aux soins, cette initiative s’inscrit dans une démarche de prévention et de responsabilisation face à des maladies dont les conséquences peuvent être dramatiques lorsqu’elles sont détectées tardivement. Au cœur des échanges, Dr Havanatou Camara, gynécologue-obstétricienne à la retraite, a délivré un message sans équivoque : le dépistage précoce constitue une étape essentielle pour détecter les lésions précancéreuses, identifier les cancers à un stade précoce et améliorer les chances de traitement. Avec des mots simples, mais empreints d’une profonde conviction, la spécialiste a invité les femmes à ne pas attendre l’apparition de symptômes graves avant de consulter. « Toutes les femmes à partir de 25 ans doivent aller dans une structure où l’on peut faire le dépistage du cancer du col », a-t-elle recommandé, en insistant sur l’importance d’une prise en charge rapide lorsque les résultats révèlent une anomalie. Pour elle, la lutte contre le cancer du col de l’utérus exige avant tout une mobilisation collective, une meilleure connaissance des moyens de prévention et un accès effectif aux services de dépistage et de soins. Son intervention a également été marquée par un appel à dépasser la gêne et les préjugés qui éloignent encore certaines femmes des structures sanitaires. « Ne vous gênez pas, ne vous découragez pas », a-t-elle lancé, encourageant les participantes à se tourner vers des professionnels qualifiés, capables de les accompagner dans le dépistage et, si nécessaire, dans la prise en charge médicale. La gynécologue-obstétricienne a par ailleurs salué l’initiative de la direction générale d’AGEROUTE Guinée, qu’elle considère comme une occasion importante de rapprocher l’information sanitaire des travailleuses et travailleurs. Au-delà du cadre professionnel, elle souhaite voir ce type de sensibilisation toucher un public plus large, afin que les connaissances acquises deviennent un véritable outil de prévention au sein des familles et des communautés. A l’issue de cette rencontre, Malick Bangoura, chef du service juridique et contentieux à AGEROUTE Guinée, s’est réjoui de la qualité des enseignements reçus. Au nom de cette volonté de faire de la prévention une responsabilité partagée, il a salué l’initiative de la direction générale, qui a permis aux participants de mieux comprendre les causes du cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus, les mesures de prévention ainsi que les conséquences d’un défaut de prise en charge à temps. Pour lui, la satisfaction exprimée à l’issue de la séance doit désormais se traduire par des actions concrètes. Dans un contexte où l’information peut contribuer à sauver des vies, chaque participant est appelé à devenir un relais auprès de ses proches, de ses connaissances et de son entourage. Il a ainsi plaidé pour la multiplication de telles initiatives, tout en évoquant la nécessité d’approfondir la réflexion sur la question et d’encourager une contribution accrue du secteur privé aux efforts de prévention. Cette volonté de transmettre l’information trouve un écho particulier chez Aïcha Condé, chargée de projets à AGEROUTE Guinée. Marquée par les explications de Dr Havanatou Camara, elle reconnaît avoir pris davantage conscience des dangers liés à ces maladies et de l’importance du dépistage, y compris chez les femmes instruites. « Je suis sûre que je vais aller directement au centre de dépistage », confie-t-elle, déterminée à mettre en pratique les enseignements reçus. Son témoignage traduit l’un des objectifs majeurs de la rencontre : transformer la sensibilisation en une décision personnelle, puis cette décision en un réflexe durable de prévention. Consciente des réalités sociales et familiales auxquelles de nombreuses femmes sont confrontées, Aïcha Condé souhaite également porter ce message au-delà de son lieu de travail. Elle exhorte les femmes de Guinée à dépasser leurs appréhensions et à faire de leur santé une priorité. Pour elle, le dépistage ne doit être ni une source de honte ni une démarche que l’on repousse à plus tard, mais un acte de responsabilité envers soi-même et sa famille. Le même sentiment de prise de conscience anime Margueritte Loua, stagiaire à la Direction administrative et des ressources humaines d’AGEROUTE Guinée. Si le cancer est une maladie dont elle avait déjà entendu parler, les explications détaillées sur ses manifestations et ses conséquences lui ont permis de mieux mesurer les risques et l’importance d’une vigilance accrue. Elle retient notamment qu’il ne faut pas attendre que la maladie se manifeste à un stade avancé pour agir. Son appel à effectuer des examens de dépistage résume l’esprit de cette rencontre : mieux connaître la maladie pour mieux la prévenir, et diffuser les informations essentielles afin de protéger les personnes exposées. En ouvrant ses portes à cette initiative de sensibilisation, AGEROUTE Guinée rappelle ainsi que la responsabilité d’une institution ne se limite pas à ses missions professionnelles. Elle peut aussi s’exprimer à travers des actions qui contribuent au bien-être de son personnel et à la diffusion de messages d’intérêt public. Au terme de cette rencontre, les participants repartent avec des connaissances renforcées, mais surtout avec un engagement : faire circuler l’information et encourager les femmes à franchir le pas du dépistage. Car face au cancer, le silence et l’attente peuvent coûter cher, tandis que l’information, la prévention et une prise en charge précoce peuvent faire toute la différence. A AGEROUTE Guinée, le message est désormais clair : se faire dépister, c’est agir à temps ; sensibiliser, c’est contribuer à sauver des vies.

Recours du Hafia FC devant le TAS : le Tribunal Arbitral du Sport ordonne le report de la confrontation AS Douanes – CR Belouizdad demandé par le Hafia FC
items.description: Le Hafia Football Club informe ses supporters, ses partenaires et l'opinion sportive que le Tribunal Arbitral du Sport (TAS), saisi de son recours contre la décision de la Confédération Africaine de Football (CAF) de faire rejouer le match retour du premier tour préliminaire de la Coupe de la Confédération CAF 2026/2027 contre l'AS Douanes (Mauritanie), a rendu ce vendredi 16 octobre 2026 une ordonnance de mesures provisionnelles dans l'affaire TAS 2026/A/12858. Après examen de la requête du Hafia FC, le TAS a ordonné à la CAF de reporter la double confrontation du deuxième tour préliminaire opposant l'AS Douanes au CR Belouizdad (Algérie), initialement prévue le 17 octobre 2026 (aller) et du 23 au 25 octobre 2026 (retour). Le Tribunal a notamment relevé que la décision de la CAF retenant la force majeure ne comportait aucune motivation, et que l'appel interne du club devant le Jury d'Appel de la CAF, introduit dès le 16 septembre 2026, était resté sans réponse. Cette ordonnance constitue une victoire importante pour le Hafia FC. Elle préserve pleinement les droits du club dans la suite de la procédure et garantit qu'une décision favorable au fond ne sera pas privée d'effet par un fait accompli sportif. Le Hafia FC maintient sa contestation d'une décision de la CAF qu'il estime non fondée, la non-présentation de l'AS Douanes à Conakry le 11 septembre 2026 relevant selon lui de défaillances organisationnelles évitables et non d'un cas de force majeure. La procédure au fond se poursuit devant le TAS. Le Hafia FC tiendra le public informé de chaque nouvelle étape et remercie ses supporters pour leur soutien constant et leur patience. La Direction du Hafia Football Club

items.title: PM Shehbaz reaffirms support for Saudi Arabia in meeting with new envoy
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its “sovereignty, security and territorial integrity” amid a recent escalation in Houthi attacks. According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), the premier made the remarks during a meeting with newly appointed Saudi Ambassador Dr Rajeh Tami Albugamy. He welcomed the envoy to Pakistan and congratulated him on assuming his new responsibilities. Ambassador Albugamy, assumed his diplomatic responsibilities in Islamabad on Thursday, reaffirming the commitment to strengthening the strategic and fraternal ties between the two countries. During the meeting, PM Shehbaz said Pakistan-Saudi Arabia relations had made significant progress in recent years and reaffirmed Islamabad’s commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation across various sectors. He “strongly condemned” the recent escalation in Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, which had resulted in deaths and injuries, including among Pakistani nationals, the statement said. The prime minister also said the two countries had always stood by each other, adding that the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and the Makkah Joint Defence Alliance marked “historic milestones” in their longstanding fraternal relations and reflected their shared commitment to regional peace and security. PM Shehbaz also thanked the Saudi leadership for its longstanding economic and financial support to Pakistan and assured the ambassador of Pakistan’s full support and cooperation in further strengthening bilateral ties. Ambassador Albugamy also met Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, where the latter underscored longstanding fraternal and strategic ties between Islamabad and Riyadh, according to the Foreign Office (FO). He also reaffirmed Pakistan and Saudi Arabia’s “shared commitment to further strengthen bilateral cooperation for mutual progress and prosperity”. The FO added that the new Saudi envoy conveyed greetings from the kingdom’s leadership to Pakistan, with Dar reciprocating and conveying his best wishes to Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and other Saudi leaders. The meeting comes amid heightened tensions in the Middle East. On Wednesday, Yemen’s Houthi rebels said they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco, after Saudi officials reported a strike on a building in Riyadh housing the energy giant’s operations centre. Powerful explosions also rattled the Saudi capital, as the coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a missile fired by the group towards Riyadh. On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia launched strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, targeting fuel and energy facilities it said were being used to support missile and drone attacks, as the Yemeni group threatened a “harsh and painful” response against Saudi airports, refineries and oil installations. Hours later, Saudi authorities issued warnings of potential hostile aerial threats in the kingdom’s eastern province and Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, according to witnesses. Later, a Saudi energy ministry official confirmed the attack. Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said that four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital and that 15 homes were damaged. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July. Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On October 5, in an emergency meeting of the Makkah pact in Riyadh, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, maintained that Pakistan and Turkiye had “presence in theatre” and only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

items.title: Contrôle des prix: deux caves et cinq maquis ont été scellés dans le Bankui
items.description: (Pâ, le 16 octobre 2026) Du 8 au 14 octobre 2026, la Direction régionale de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat du Bankui (DRICA-BNK) a mené une vaste opération de contrôle des prix à Poura et à Pa. Au total, 275 points de vente ont été inspectés afin de lutter contre les pratiques spéculatives sur les produits de grande consommation et de veiller au respect de la réglementation commerciale. Cette opération a permis de constater des manquements liés à la vente de bière au-delà des tarifs réglementaires. En conséquence, deux caves et cinq maquis ont été scellés. Les commerçants concernés ont également fait l’objet de sanctions. À travers cette opération, la DRICA-BNK rappelle qu’aucune augmentation des prix de la bière n’a été décidée. Elle invite les tenanciers de caves et de maquis à respecter strictement les tarifs en vigueur, sous peine de sanctions conformément à la réglementation. La DRICA-BNK réaffirme ainsi sa vigilance dans la lutte contre les pratiques commerciales illicites et appelle les acteurs du commerce à faire preuve de responsabilité afin de préserver les intérêts des consommateurs.
